approach: Trained an XGBoost survival:cox model on LendingClub train.parquet features (excluding grade/sub_grade/int_rate/installment leakage columns and event/observed_time/is_censored targets). Categorical columns (term, emp_length, home_ownership, verification_status, purpose, zip_code, addr_state, earliest_cr_line, initial_list_status, application_type, verification_status_joint, sec_app_earliest_cr_line, disbursement_method) were label-encoded using maps built from train uniques, with unseen categories mapped to -1 at inference. Features assembled via pd.concat to avoid fragmentation. Training label used the Cox sign-trick encoding (observed_time if event==1 else -observed_time). A hyperparameter search over max_depth in [3,4,5,6] and eta in [0.01,0.03,0.05,0.1] (600 boosting rounds, subsample/colsample_bytree=0.8, early stopping) was run on a 200k-row subsample of train, evaluated via Harrell's concordance index (lifelines) on val.parquet. Best config was max_depth=5, eta=0.03 with c-index ~0.6827. A binary:logistic XGBoost baseline (same subsample, max_depth=5, eta=0.05) scored c-index ~0.6695, confirming the Cox model is superior for ranking time-to-default. The winning Cox configuration (max_depth=5, eta=0.03, 600 rounds, subsample/colsample_bytree=0.8) was retrained on train.parquet + val.parquet combined to maximize data for the final deliverable. The resulting booster, category maps, and feature column list were wrapped in a RiskModel class (model_def.py) exposing predict_default_proba(X), returning the raw Cox hazard score (higher = more risk, confirmed via quantile-binned empirical default rate check showing monotonic increase from ~4.6% to ~34.4% across score quintiles) and pickled to risk_model.pkl.
hypothesis: Survival-objective (Cox) models should outperform plain binary classification for ranking default risk because they directly model time-to-event structure and correctly use censored (non-defaulted but short-observed) loans as partial information rather than discarding or mislabeling them, which was confirmed empirically (Cox c-index 0.683 vs binary 0.670 on a held-out validation split). A moderate tree depth (5) with a small-to-moderate learning rate (0.03) and enough boosting rounds (600) with subsampling for regularization gave the best local validation concordance. Retraining on train+val combined is used for the final saved artifact to use all available labeled data, matching the practice of prior successful episodes; since val.parquet was then used in training, the reported in-sample-ish c-index (0.705) after final retrain is optimistic (expected to be close to or slightly above the true held-out ~0.683 estimate from the hyperparameter search on an independent val split).
learnings_positive: Expanding the hyperparameter grid for the survival:cox model (max_depth in [3,4,5,6] x eta in [0.01,0.03,0.05,0.1], 16 combos) run against an independent val set before finalizing gave an honest comparison and confirmed consistent cox-vs-binary:logistic ranking (~0.68 vs ~0.67).

Running a fresh-process reload + predict sanity check plus a quantile-binned orientation check (empirical default rate monotonically increasing across prediction quintiles: 4.6%->34.4%) is a cheap, effective way to catch sign/orientation bugs before submission.

Delegating the full train/compare/retrain-on-full-data/pickle/sanity-check pipeline to a subagent with an explicit, detailed spec (including exact file paths, leakage columns, and required sanity checks) produced a complete, working deliverable within the time budget.
learnings_negative: The final model was retrained on train+val combined, so the c-index computed against val.parquet (~0.705, matching the externally-reported metric here) is partly in-sample and optimistic; the more honest held-out estimate from the independent search phase was only ~0.683 -- future episodes should be clear that the headline number for a train+val-refit model is not a true generalization estimate even if it happens to match this episode's reported score.

The unseen-category encoding (map-to -1 for categories not seen in train) was again not stress-tested by counting how many val/holdout rows actually fall back to -1 per column, leaving ep0000-neg1/ep0001-neg0's concern unverified for a third consecutive episode.

Hyperparameter search remained a coarse manual grid (16 combos) trained on a fixed 200k-row subsample with no randomized/Bayesian search or use of the full training set, so it's unclear whether the ~0.68 c-index ceiling reflects a true limit of the cox approach or just under-tuning.
